\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{sec:extended_discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations---establishes that this boundary is remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B scale.

The shallowness is explained by the rate of information loss.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$), reflecting the large distributional gap between human and first-generation text.
At 1v2, $\auc$ drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp (range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all conditions), indicating that the majority of discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By 2v3, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.

This pattern aligns with model collapse findings.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating predictable tail probability mass loss.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that operationally, this approach is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

The consistency across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy, nucleus ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ in $[0.6866, 0.7039]$.
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength but does not shift the boundary, suggesting that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the information bottleneck of the generation process rather than sampling algorithm properties.

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer Implications}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retains 90--92\% accuracy, and broader continuation-mode transfer shows 80--92\% retention across all pairs.
At 0v1, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 for all pairs, confirming fully transferable binary contamination detection.

A single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed for texts from other models without retraining---extending utility to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown.

Two caveats: (1)~a nontrivial model-specific residual persists despite high transfer, and (2)~Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is consistent across decoding strategies, feature importance ordering varies.
Greedy and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with vocabulary diversity measures dominating.
Greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction).
$T{=}1.2$ promotes \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to top ranks; \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 (greedy) to rank~5.

The \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} depends on sampling strategy.
A general-purpose classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups.

\subsection{Scale Considerations}

Our $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\leq$1.5B constitutes a methodological lower bound.
All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics without model internals, and cross-model transfer (80--92\%) demonstrates methodology generalization across architectures.

Scaling to larger models presents two outcomes: if $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ (as scaling laws suggest~\cite{dohmatob2024model}), depth contamination becomes more insidious and our framework more necessary; if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists, our conclusions generalize directly.
The high cross-model transfer across three architecturally distinct families provides indirect evidence that depth signals are not tied to a specific pretraining paradigm.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:extended_llm}

On a 500-sample test set (5 depth classes), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% (MAE = 1.15)---both below OBD-LightGBM's 38.6\% (Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
Both achieve ${\sim}$88\% binary accuracy.

Per-depth analysis: both models achieve high depth-0 recall (GPT-5.5: 0.77, Claude: 0.69) but recall for depths 1--4 collapses to 0.08--0.38, with predictions scattered nearly uniformly across non-human classes.
Spearman correlations are weak ($\rho = 0.38$, $0.42$), confirming that frontier LLMs function as binary detectors augmented by near-random depth guessing.

Statistical detection methods (DetectGPT~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt}, Binoculars~\cite{hans2024binoculars}) optimize scalar scores for the binary boundary---the same distinction where LLM baselines excel.
But the per-depth recall collapse demonstrates that binary detection confidence is orthogonal to generational depth.

\subsection{Broader Impact}

The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled text---a one-wash laundering effect that limits filtering granularity.

$\Kstar$ provides a corpus audit metric: what fraction of a training corpus consists of depth-$\geq 2$ text?
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic without expensive retraining experiments.

\subsection{Degradation and Practical Considerations}

In our continual training experiments (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}), all strategies degrade the base model's general capabilities (MMLU: 0.6018 $\to$ 0.5865--0.5941; HellaSwag: 0.6821 $\to$ 0.6638--0.6701).
This must be interpreted in context: our 100\% synthetic setting provides an upper-bound characterization.
In realistic mixed-corpus settings, degradation is proportional to the contamination fraction~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
Even under this extreme condition, $\Kstar$-aware binary filtering reduces MMLU degradation from $-$1.53\,pp to $-$0.77\,pp---an approximately 50\% reduction.

Binary filtering at the $\Kstar = 2$ boundary requires no per-model calibration, is simple to implement, and is universally applicable across tested generator configurations.
Combining depth-aware filtering with distribution-matching methods (DSIR, DoReMi) is a promising direction.

\subsection{Extended Limitations}
\label{sec:extended_limitations}

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our prompt-chain protocol holds model quality constant; real-world retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics.
Under the monotonic-degradation assumption~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}, $\Kstar^{\text{retrain}} \leq \Kstar^{\text{prompt}}$, making our $\Kempirical = 2$ a conservative estimate.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
At $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 3$ uniformly.
At $\theta = 0.65$, continuation-mode configurations drop to $\Kempirical = 1$ while rewrite retains $\Kempirical = 2$.
At $\theta = 0.70$, $\Kempirical = 1$ universally.
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.15\,pp; Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by 0.09\,pp.
All eight boundary comparisons yield permutation $p < 0.01$.

\emph{Graduated filtering.}
Graduated filtering at all tested $\alpha$ values (0.1--0.9) underperforms binary-ours on MMLU (best: $0.5892$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$ vs.\ $0.5941$), with a monotonic trend.
At $\alpha{=}0.9$, HellaSwag matches binary-ours exactly ($0.6701$), consistent with $\Kempirical = 2$ predicting no benefit from finer ordinal structure.

-We now show that this characterization is not merely descriptive but \emph{predictive}: $\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit over binary filtering.

+We compare six data curation strategies on a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth, depths 0--5): (i)~\textbf{no-filter} (uniform weight), (ii)~\textbf{binary-ours} ($w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$ from the 15D LightGBM classifier), (iii)~\textbf{binary-Drayson} (importance weighting following \citet{drayson2025}, same classifier, weights $w_j \propto (1 - q(x_j))^b$, $b{=}1$, cap $r_{\max}{=}3$), (iv)~\textbf{graduated} (exponential decay $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, $\alpha \in \{0.1,\ldots,0.9\}$), (v)~\textbf{surprisal} (retain documents above corpus median surprisal), and (vi)~\textbf{DSIR}~\citep{xie2023dsir} (importance resampling against depth-0 reference).

lines: -Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.

-Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
-Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
-Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.

-Further work shows that even a vanishingly small fraction of synthetic data suffices to trigger collapse, with the effect amplified in larger models~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}; their distribution-shift analysis and our information-theoretic derivation of $\Kstar$ arrive at the same conclusion from complementary starting points---recursive generation inevitably degrades information to a finite boundary.
-Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.

-Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.

-Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
-Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
-Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.

-Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} proved that collapse is avoidable when sufficient original data is retained alongside synthetic samples, a condition that depth-aware curation can enforce by construction.
-These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

The gap cuts across three communities.
Binary detection methods~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp, zawalski2026codec} produce no depth estimate.
The model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} characterizes recursive degradation at the macro level but provides no per-text depth estimation tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations---using 15 statistical features and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k$ where the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc_{k,k+1}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$.

Our primary contribution is a systematic empirical characterization of $\Kempirical$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{$\Kempirical = 2$} across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions), with all 1v2 CI lower bounds exceeding $\theta$ and all 2v3 CI upper bounds below $\theta$ (permutation $p \leq 0.002$).
  \item \textbf{Cross-model transfer}: 80--92\% accuracy retention across continuation-mode generators; 0v1 $\auc > 0.96$ across all pairs.
  \item \textbf{Feature degradation consistency}: Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ on single-feature rankings across continuation-mode models, with surprisal-variance features dominating.
  \item \textbf{Generation mode}: rewrite yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ ($+$8.4\,pp) but transfers poorly (61--63\% vs.\ 80--92\%).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a secondary contribution, $\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit: graduated filtering at its best ($\alpha{=}0.9$, MMLU $0.5892$) still falls short of binary-ours ($0.5941$), and surprisal-based selection ($0.5894$) likewise fails to improve (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented the first systematic measurement of the generational depth discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ for recursive synthetic text.
Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total) at the $\leq$1.5B scale, $\Kempirical = 2$ is consistent: all 1v2 bootstrap CI lower bounds exceed $\theta = 0.60$ (permutation $p \leq 0.002$) while all 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below it.
Cross-model transfer retains 80--92\% accuracy across continuation-mode generators, with 0v1 $\auc > 0.96$ across all pairs, indicating that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
A preliminary neural probe yields $\Kempirical^{\text{neural}} = 3$ on one dataset, confirming that $\Kempirical = 2$ is a representation-dependent lower bound.

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit: binary filtering ($0.5941$ MMLU) outperforms graduated depth weighting ($0.5892$ at best $\alpha$) and surprisal-based selection ($0.5894$), establishing $\Kempirical$ as an actionable curation guideline.

Key directions for future work include scaling to 7B+ models, extending to multilingual and multi-domain corpora, establishing the prompt-chain vs.\ retrain-chain $\Kstar$ relationship, and cross-model validation of the neural probe boundary.

2	\label{sec:filtering}
3	
4	$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement beyond the binary boundary provides no additional benefit over binary filtering.
5	We compare six data curation strategies on a corpus of 30{,}000 documents (5{,}000 per depth, depths 0--5): (i)~\textbf{no-filter} (uniform weight), (ii)~\textbf{binary-ours} ($w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$ from the 15D LightGBM classifier), (iii)~\textbf{binary-Drayson} (importance weighting following \citet{drayson2025}, same classifier, weights $w_j \propto (1 - q(x_j))^b$, $b{=}1$, cap $r_{\max}{=}3$), (iv)~\textbf{graduated} (exponential decay $w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, $\alpha \in \{0.1,\ldots,0.9\}$), (v)~\textbf{surprisal} (retain documents above corpus median surprisal), and (vi)~\textbf{DSIR}~\citep{xie2023dsir} (importance resampling against depth-0 reference).
6	
7	We fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (rank~8, $\alpha_{\text{LoRA}}{=}16$) for 3 epochs, evaluating on MMLU (14{,}042 examples, 0-shot) and HellaSwag (10{,}042 examples, 0-shot) across 5 seeds; the graduated strategy is further crossed with 5~$\alpha$ values (51 total runs).

10	
11	\input{tables/tab_filtering_main}

13	All strategies degrade absolute performance relative to the base model (MMLU 0.6018, HellaSwag 0.6821).

20	Higher $\alpha$ values yield monotonically better performance on both benchmarks (HellaSwag: $0.6640$ at $\alpha{=}0.1$ to $0.6701$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$).

25	$\Kempirical = 2$ correctly predicts that graduated refinement provides no additional benefit.

2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Interpretation.}

9

1	\section{Extended Discussion}
2	\label{sec:extended_discussion}
3	
4	\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
5	
6	The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
7	Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations---establishes that this boundary is remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B scale.
8	
9	The shallowness is explained by the rate of information loss.
10	The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$), reflecting the large distributional gap between human and first-generation text.
11	At 1v2, $\auc$ drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp (range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all conditions), indicating that the majority of discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
12	By 2v3, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
13	
14	This pattern aligns with model collapse findings.
15	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations.
16	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating predictable tail probability mass loss.
17	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that operationally, this approach is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.
18	
19	The consistency across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
20	Greedy, nucleus ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ in $[0.6866, 0.7039]$.
21	Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength but does not shift the boundary, suggesting that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the information bottleneck of the generation process rather than sampling algorithm properties.
22	
23	\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer Implications}
24	
25	The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
26	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retains 90--92\% accuracy, and broader continuation-mode transfer shows 80--92\% retention across all pairs.
27	At 0v1, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 for all pairs, confirming fully transferable binary contamination detection.
28	
29	A single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed for texts from other models without retraining---extending utility to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown.
30	
31	Two caveats: (1)~a nontrivial model-specific residual persists despite high transfer, and (2)~Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.
32	
33	\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
34	
35	While $\Kempirical = 2$ is consistent across decoding strategies, feature importance ordering varies.
36	Greedy and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with vocabulary diversity measures dominating.
37	Greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction).
38	$T{=}1.2$ promotes \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to top ranks; \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 (greedy) to rank~5.
39	
40	The \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} depends on sampling strategy.
41	A general-purpose classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups.
42	
43	\subsection{Scale Considerations}
44	
45	Our $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\leq$1.5B constitutes a methodological lower bound.
46	All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics without model internals, and cross-model transfer (80--92\%) demonstrates methodology generalization across architectures.
47	
48	Scaling to larger models presents two outcomes: if $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ (as scaling laws suggest~\cite{dohmatob2024model}), depth contamination becomes more insidious and our framework more necessary; if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists, our conclusions generalize directly.
49	The high cross-model transfer across three architecturally distinct families provides indirect evidence that depth signals are not tied to a specific pretraining paradigm.
50	
51	\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
52	\label{sec:extended_llm}
53	
54	On a 500-sample test set (5 depth classes), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% (MAE = 1.15)---both below OBD-LightGBM's 38.6\% (Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
55	Both achieve ${\sim}$88\% binary accuracy.
56	
57	Per-depth analysis: both models achieve high depth-0 recall (GPT-5.5: 0.77, Claude: 0.69) but recall for depths 1--4 collapses to 0.08--0.38, with predictions scattered nearly uniformly across non-human classes.
58	Spearman correlations are weak ($\rho = 0.38$, $0.42$), confirming that frontier LLMs function as binary detectors augmented by near-random depth guessing.
59	
60	Statistical detection methods (DetectGPT~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt}, Binoculars~\cite{hans2024binoculars}) optimize scalar scores for the binary boundary---the same distinction where LLM baselines excel.
61	But the per-depth recall collapse demonstrates that binary detection confidence is orthogonal to generational depth.
62	
63	\subsection{Broader Impact}
64	
65	The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
66	A single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled text---a one-wash laundering effect that limits filtering granularity.
67	
68	$\Kstar$ provides a corpus audit metric: what fraction of a training corpus consists of depth-$\geq 2$ text?
69	If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic without expensive retraining experiments.
70	
71	\subsection{Degradation and Practical Considerations}
72	
73	In our continual training experiments (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}), all strategies degrade the base model's general capabilities (MMLU: 0.6018 $\to$ 0.5865--0.5941; HellaSwag: 0.6821 $\to$ 0.6638--0.6701).
74	This must be interpreted in context: our 100\% synthetic setting provides an upper-bound characterization.
75	In realistic mixed-corpus settings, degradation is proportional to the contamination fraction~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.

\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{sec:extended_discussion}

\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ consistently across all 8 tested configurations---establishes that this boundary is remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B scale.

The shallowness is explained by the rate of information loss.
The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$), reflecting the large distributional gap between human and first-generation text.
At 1v2, $\auc$ drops by ${\sim}$30\,pp (range: 0.6112--0.7039 across all conditions), indicating that the majority of discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
By 2v3, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.

This pattern aligns with model collapse findings.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating predictable tail probability mass loss.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that operationally, this approach is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

The consistency across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy, nucleus ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$ (Table~\ref{tab:s2_decoding}), with 1v2 $\auc$ in $[0.6866, 0.7039]$.
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength but does not shift the boundary, suggesting that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the information bottleneck of the generation process rather than sampling algorithm properties.

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer Implications}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retains 90--92\% accuracy, and broader continuation-mode transfer shows 80--92\% retention across all pairs.
At 0v1, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 for all pairs, confirming fully transferable binary contamination detection.

A single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed for texts from other models without retraining---extending utility to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown.

Two caveats: (1)~a nontrivial model-specific residual persists despite high transfer, and (2)~Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is consistent across decoding strategies, feature importance ordering varies.
Greedy and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with vocabulary diversity measures dominating.
Greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction).
$T{=}1.2$ promotes \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to top ranks; \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 (greedy) to rank~5.

The \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} depends on sampling strategy.
A general-purpose classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups.

\subsection{Scale Considerations}

Our $\Kempirical = 2$ at $\leq$1.5B constitutes a methodological lower bound.
All 15 features are computed from surface-level token statistics without model internals, and cross-model transfer (80--92\%) demonstrates methodology generalization across architectures.

Scaling to larger models presents two outcomes: if $\Kempirical > 2$ at 7B+ (as scaling laws suggest~\cite{dohmatob2024model}), depth contamination becomes more insidious and our framework more necessary; if $\Kempirical = 2$ persists, our conclusions generalize directly.
The high cross-model transfer across three architecturally distinct families provides indirect evidence that depth signals are not tied to a specific pretraining paradigm.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:extended_llm}

On a 500-sample test set (5 depth classes), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% (MAE = 1.15)---both below OBD-LightGBM's 38.6\% (Table~\ref{tab:s3_llm_zeroshot}).
Both achieve ${\sim}$88\% binary accuracy.

Per-depth analysis: both models achieve high depth-0 recall (GPT-5.5: 0.77, Claude: 0.69) but recall for depths 1--4 collapses to 0.08--0.38, with predictions scattered nearly uniformly across non-human classes.
Spearman correlations are weak ($\rho = 0.38$, $0.42$), confirming that frontier LLMs function as binary detectors augmented by near-random depth guessing.

Statistical detection methods (DetectGPT~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt}, Binoculars~\cite{hans2024binoculars}) optimize scalar scores for the binary boundary---the same distinction where LLM baselines excel.
But the per-depth recall collapse demonstrates that binary detection confidence is orthogonal to generational depth.

\subsection{Broader Impact}

The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
A single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from multiply recycled text---a one-wash laundering effect that limits filtering granularity.

$\Kstar$ provides a corpus audit metric: what fraction of a training corpus consists of depth-$\geq 2$ text?
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic without expensive retraining experiments.

\subsection{Degradation and Practical Considerations}

In our continual training experiments (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}), all strategies degrade the base model's general capabilities (MMLU: 0.6018 $\to$ 0.5865--0.5941; HellaSwag: 0.6821 $\to$ 0.6638--0.6701).
This must be interpreted in context: our 100\% synthetic setting provides an upper-bound characterization.
In realistic mixed-corpus settings, degradation is proportional to the contamination fraction~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
Even under this extreme condition, $\Kstar$-aware binary filtering reduces MMLU degradation from $-$1.53\,pp to $-$0.77\,pp---an approximately 50\% reduction.

Binary filtering at the $\Kstar = 2$ boundary requires no per-model calibration, is simple to implement, and is universally applicable across tested generator configurations.
Combining depth-aware filtering with distribution-matching methods (DSIR, DoReMi) is a promising direction.

\subsection{Extended Limitations}
\label{sec:extended_limitations}

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our prompt-chain protocol holds model quality constant; real-world retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics.
Under the monotonic-degradation assumption~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}, $\Kstar^{\text{retrain}} \leq \Kstar^{\text{prompt}}$, making our $\Kempirical = 2$ a conservative estimate.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
At $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 3$ uniformly.
At $\theta = 0.65$, continuation-mode configurations drop to $\Kempirical = 1$ while rewrite retains $\Kempirical = 2$.
At $\theta = 0.70$, $\Kempirical = 1$ universally.
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.15\,pp; Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by 0.09\,pp.
All eight boundary comparisons yield permutation $p < 0.01$.

\emph{Graduated filtering.}
Graduated filtering at all tested $\alpha$ values (0.1--0.9) underperforms binary-ours on MMLU (best: $0.5892$ at $\alpha{=}0.9$ vs.\ $0.5941$), with a monotonic trend.
At $\alpha{=}0.9$, HellaSwag matches binary-ours exactly ($0.6701$), consistent with $\Kempirical = 2$ predicting no benefit from finer ordinal structure.
